analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to state explicitly when federal law overrides state and local rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was referred to and died when the 104th Congress ended, without a vote or a cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed how federal law interacts with state and local laws. As a default rule, a federal statute would no longer wipe out state or local rules unless Congress said so in plain words, or unless the two directly conflict and cannot stand together. It would also require the Congressional Research Service, the research arm of Congress, to publish a report after each Congress listing every new federal preemption of state and local power, and send it to the President and committee chairmen.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local governments, which would keep their police powers, zoning rules, consumer protections, and local ordinances unless Congress expressly said otherwise. Courts deciding preemption cases would have a clearer default rule, and the public would get a published inventory of every new federal override of state law.

how_it_helps.text: No federal statute or rule would preempt state or local law unless the statute explicitly says preemption is intended, or unless the two directly conflict and cannot be reconciled [S2] [S3].

The Congressional Research Service would publish, within 90 days after each Congress ends, a public report listing federal statutes that preempt state and local powers, summarizing new preemptive legislation, and reviewing recent preemption court cases [S2] [S3].

The bill's stated findings argue that unclear preemption leaves too much discretion to federal agencies, creates uncertainty for state and local governments, and lets courts decide the scope of preemption in ways sometimes beyond Congress's intent [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Congress and federal agencies, which would have to write preemption intentions explicitly and lose the ability to rely on courts finding implied preemption. Businesses that prefer one uniform federal standard would face more patchworks of differing state and local rules.

drawbacks.text: Many federal statutes do not state preemption explicitly, and courts have long read preemption into them; a rigid rule could invite litigation over what counts as a 'direct conflict' and complicate drafting [S3].

National businesses and industries argue that uniform federal standards prevent a patchwork of 50 differing state rules, which can raise compliance costs that get passed to consumers; this bill would make such patchworks harder to preempt away [S3].
The default rule could also cut both ways: it would protect state laws that are stronger than federal standards, but also make it harder to displace state rules that interfere with federal programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real ambiguity in federalism — courts often find preemption Congress never clearly stated — and its reporting requirement was a low-cost transparency measure. But it was a broad interpretive rule with few supporters, and its effect on ordinary people is indirect: states would gain power, which could mean stronger local protections in some states and a more fragmented regulatory map in others.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, which never acted on it before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Carl Levin introduced the bill on April 17, 1996, with introductory remarks in the Congressional Record [S1] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs on April 17, 1996; no further action was taken [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo: Congress and federal agencies kept the ability to rely on implied preemption found by courts, and industries that benefit from uniform federal standards overriding state rules were spared a default rule favoring state and local authority.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal agencies and industries relying on federal preemption

for.name: Sen. Carl Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was referred to committee

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup, hearing, or floor vote

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have preserved state and local authority over ordinances, regulations, and police powers unless Congress stated preemption explicitly, and would have given them a clearer legal default. The public would also gain a published record of every new federal override of state law.
The bill would have forced Congress to state preemption intentions explicitly and curtailed the discretion of federal agencies whose regulations have been construed to preempt state law.

Industries that benefit when one federal standard overrides a patchwork of state rules would find it harder to obtain preemption; industries that already comply with diverse state rules would be unaffected. The effect on consumers runs both directions depending on whether state or federal rules are stronger.
